newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks, bonds fall sharply in nervous trade.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks, bonds fall sharply in nervous trade.

text.p: U.S. stocks and bonds fell sharply Tuesday after news the U.S. had fired cruise missiles at Iraqi targets coincided with new fears that short term interest rates might rise more than previously thought.
"I think Saddam Hussein is testing us," said a trader as stock prices moved broadly lower. Stocks of oil companies and oil drillers bucked the trend and posted gains.
"We continue to have a view that the Federal Reserve will tighten at the September 24 meeting," said Lehman Brothers strategist Jeffrey Applegate.
U.S. stocks were off their lows after news at 1000 EDT/1400 that the National Association of Purchasing Management index in August rose to 52.6, in line with expectations.
Bonds were also off early lows, with the 30-year issue down 5/32 and the yield falling to 7.13 percent after the early decline had pushed it to around 7.18 percent.

The New York Stock Exchange imposed curbs on program trading eight minutes into the trading day with the Dow down 50 points to 5566. The curbs were lifted an hour later as the Dow bounced from the early lows.
The Dow industrials were down about 25 to 5592 at 1100 EDT/1500 GMT, equivalent to a drop of 0.43 percent.
The dollar gained on the yen, opening at 109.35/40 yen in New York. The mark also rose against the yen, while the dollar/mark rate was steady with an opening at 1.4860/70 marks in New York.
After initial strength, December gold traded at the COMEX in New York fell $0.20 an ounce to $391.10. Oil prices soared on world markets amid the U.S.-Iraqi confrontation.
Chevron, Texaco and Exxon, the three oil stocks in the Dow, were each up more than $1 a share in mid-morning.

"The market is going to be very schizophrenic" between now and the September 24 meeting of the Fed's policy setting group, said Trude Latimer, an independent analyst. She said any predictions about rate moves from well-known forecasters will get close attention. She said cash levels are not as plentiful as they were last year and some money managers will be inclined to sell into any strength if stocks move higher.

Lehman's Applegate said the markets are "repricing" for the possibility the Fed will boost short-term rates one-half a percentage point instead of the quarter-point increase that many thought might be coming.
Marchall Acuff, stategist at Smith Barney, noted that bonds and the stock averages were off their lows while "the broad market is pretty weak."

He said the Mid-East situation "can come and go" as a market factor. "I don't think at this point that this is the type of thing we were dealing with in the summer of 1990," he said. He added that Iraq's invasion of Kuwait that year was "a major surprise" while the current situation "at the moment looks like an event."

Just prior to the Kuwait invastion, the Dow industrials were at the 2899 level. They finished 1990 at 2629 after dipping beneath 2400 in October. The decline from a mid-1990 peak near 3000 to the year's low represented a 21 percent decline, noted William LeFevre of Ehrenkrantz King Nussbaum.
On January 17, 1991, in response to news that the U.S. and its allies launched air strikes on Iraq, the Dow rose 114 points to 2623. It ended 1991 at 3169.
"What happened in 1990/91 and what's happening in 1996 are two different events," said LeFevre. "There's not a parallel and don't look for it in the marketplace."
This Friday's scheduled release of August payroll data will be a key to determining Fed actions, the analysts said.
